sources.citation: Austronesian Basic Vocabulary Database (ABVD), language 23 'Kis', source/author D. C. Laycock (bib key Laycock-23-2005, 'personal communication'; typed Peng Du, checked Simon Greenhill), 221 entries.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No statement, but 40 of 221 forms carry an acute accent (presumably Laycock's stress mark). Rough tabulation of the 35 accented single-word stems: 26 final-syllable (dəmá 'hand', kulí 'skin', keŋí 'belly', bazá 'house', sipá 'branch', putú 'fruit', bulá 'earth', yuwá 'fire', urá(ni) 'two', owá(ni) 'four', kasík 'smoke', sepám 'bad') vs 9 penultimate (domára 'star', keŋélo 'intestines', awábot 'mouth', kəŋáŋgo 'big', bəráwa 'no', úla 'rain'). Unstressed syllables often show schwa. Data only; interpretation is mine, not the source's.

sources.citation: Ross, Malcolm. 1988. Proto Oceanic and the Austronesian languages of western Melanesia. Pacific Linguistics C-98. Canberra: ANU. Schouten chain §5.2, pp. 122-132.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: open copy online; also held in print at Harvard (Widener Library (offsite storage), call number PL6201.R67 1988)
sources.harvard_location: Widener Library (offsite storage), call number PL6201 .R67 1988
sources.note: Comparative only: Kis appears in consonant/vowel reflex tables (pp. 124-131) and cognate sets; the word 'stress' occurs only for Ali/Tumleo verb alternations (p. 86, ex. 3.115). Nothing on Kis stress. p. 123 states that within the Schouten chain 'Detailed descriptions are available for Manam (Lichtenberk 1983) and Kairiru (Wivell 1981a, 1981b)' -- i.e. none for Kis.

sources.citation: Laycock, D. C. 1976. History of research in Austronesian languages: Sepik Provinces. In S. A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea area languages and language study, vol. 2: Austronesian languages, 73-93 (section 4.2.2). Pacific Linguistics C-39. Canberra: Australian National University.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No phonology content. States that Kis was first shown on a map in Laycock 1973, that 'The first new material in Sepik AN languages was collected by Laycock during fieldwork in 1970-71; it consists of brief wordlists and grammatical materials . Kairiru, Kaiep, and Kis' (p. 81), that within the eastern group 'Kairiru and Kaiep are very closely related, with Kis at a greater distance', '(Kis falls into the western group.)' [SVO word-order group], and that Kis speakers believe their forebears migrated from Manam (p. 82). The words stress/accent/tone/penult do not occur in the chapter.
